name: Ivan Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a small buying team at the head office of a company that makes car parts, brake components mostly. Five of us buy steel, rubber seals, packaging, that sort of thing, from about two hundred suppliers. A normal day is price quotes in the morning, a call with a supplier who's late, and the afternoon on purchase orders and a monthly spend report my boss Helen reads very closely.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like negotiating, even though I'm not very good at it yet, I still blink first. I like the factory visits once a month, when you see the stuff you bought turn into brake pads. What wears me out is the purchase-order system, which is about twenty years old and needs six clicks to change a delivery date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, like most things, and move on. I'm not much of a poster. At work I'd say we should still use the bits that work, like the tool that reads supplier invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. Buying stays a job for people, I keep learning to negotiate, and the five of us keep our seats. The factory's doing all right, orders from the car makers are steady, so I don't see much risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, ask Helen to let me lead one of the bigger steel contracts next year, and keep saving about 250 a month. Maybe I'd use the AI for drafting supplier emails a bit more, since it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Mildly bored by all the AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leading the steel contract mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the biggest spend we have, about forty million a year. If Helen (his boss) gave me the steel contract, I'd finally stop being the junior who only buys cardboard boxes. It would make the case for a pay rise next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that would worry you, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate's moving out in the summer, so I'd either find someone new or pay more rent. That's the closest thing to a worry. I've got about three months saved, so it's manageable.

say: AI was **overhyped**, like most things, and I'd move on without posting.
At work I'd say keep using the bits that work, like the **invoice reader**.
think: Buying stays a **job for people**, and the five of us keep our seats.
Car-maker orders are **steady**, so the factory looks safe.
do: Ask my boss to let me lead the **steel contract** next year.
Use AI a bit more for **drafting supplier emails**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by AI talk.
S0.quote: If Helen (his boss) gave me the steel contract, I'd finally stop being the junior who only buys cardboard boxes.
fieldNote: His main ambition is **career progress** through bigger contracts.
His only worry is **rent** when his flatmate leaves, which is manageable.
He treats AI as a **useful tool**, not a threat, in this picture.

steps.text: Ask to lead the 40-million steel contract next year
Keep saving 250 a month into a savings account
Draft routine supplier emails with the AI assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and people need to get practical about it. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and stop arguing about whether they're good or bad. At work I'd be fairly upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, buying is literally on the card. Quotes, comparisons, purchase orders, chasing deliveries, a system can do all of that faster than us. I'd expect the team of five to become two, and as the junior I'm not sure I'm one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI properly for comparing quotes, so at least I'm the one who knows how. I'd ask Helen straight out what the plan is for the team. And I'd look at a supplier-quality job on the factory side, which means walking the line and checking parts, more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually steady, but this one has my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Helen go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book half an hour and ask her directly. I'd ask my boss Helen whether there's still a junior buyer in her plan for next year, and watch her face. She's straight, so I think she'd tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if your job looked shaky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, mostly, and the trip to visit my cousins in the autumn. I'd keep the savings growing instead. A new flatmate rather than living alone, too.

say: It's a **big shift**, and people should get practical and learn the tools.
At work I'd sound **fairly upbeat** in public.
think: **Buying** is on the card: quotes, orders and chasing deliveries all fit.
The team could shrink from five to **two**, and I'm the junior.
do: Use AI properly for **comparing quotes** so I'm the one who knows how.
Ask my boss directly about **the team's future**.
Look at a **supplier-quality job** on the factory floor.
feel: **Anxious**, because this scenario has **his name** on it.
S1.quote: I'd ask my boss Helen whether there's still a junior buyer in her plan for next year, and watch her face.
fieldNote: He immediately spotted **buying** listed on the card.
His plan B is a **factory-floor role**, where robots arrive later.
Steady by nature, he is still clear his **junior status** puts him at risk.

steps.text: Compare supplier quotes with the AI tool every week
Apply for the supplier-quality job on the factory side
Skip the autumn trip and cut eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and the government needs to sort out a safety net quickly. I'd probably say it in the group chat with my uni friends, who are all in office jobs too. At work I'd keep calm, because panicking helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think buying jobs go almost straight away. The AI can negotiate, compare, and place orders, and it won't blink first like I do. The factory floor lasts until about 2031, so if I'm on the line by then, I get a bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the supplier-quality role as fast as they'd let me, within six months. I'd find a new flatmate to keep rent low and push savings up to five months. I'd also think about moving back near my parents, where rent is half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed that gets me, there'd be no time to get good at anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say he told me engineering was safer than business. My dad told me to study engineering, and in this picture he'd be right for about three extra years. My mum would just be glad to cook for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen, actually. She's fifty and she's spent her whole career buying. If the AI does her job, she's got nowhere obvious to go, and she's been good to me.

I'd keep calm at work, because **panicking helps** no one.
think: **Buying jobs go** almost straight away, because AI can negotiate and order.
The **factory floor** lasts until about 2031, buying a little time.

fieldNote: He expects to **lose his buying job** almost immediately.
His fallback is the **factory floor**, which only buys about three years.
He worries for his **older boss** more than he expected to.

steps.text: Transfer to the supplier-quality job within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if companies are honest with their staff. I'd say it to friends and probably at work too. I'd still sound fairly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a few more years of buying, but I'd be stupid to count on it. The thinking part of buying goes by 2031, and the factory floor about 2034. So I'd want to be on the floor before 2031 and learning something even more hands-on by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask for a transfer to supplier quality and start a part-time quality engineering certificate. I'd save towards six months. I'd keep renting near work rather than buy, because I don't know where I'll be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with the fast one. I'd have a sequence of steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most hands-on job you can picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe maintenance on the brake-pad presses, the actual machines. I've watched the maintenance fitters fix a press in twenty minutes, and nobody in my office could do that. I'd need years of training, but five years is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound calm. Is that true inside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I'm the kind of person who calms down once there's a list. The list just has some scary items on it.

I'd say it at work too, still **fairly calm**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so let's plan. I'd tell my friends to stop pretending their jobs are safe. At work I'd talk about training budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could stay in buying a while and still make a move. I'd be thirty-seven when the AI arrives and forty around 2039 when the robots come. I'd want to have a trade or a technical skill by then, something the factory still needs a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for two or three years and try to get the steel contract, because it pays better and builds a cushion. Then I'd move into maintenance or quality. I'd also start saving for a flat, since ten years is long enough to need a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a quieter anxiety. Like knowing a bill is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to train, maybe one day a week, and a clear route from the office to the floor. Most office staff at our factory have never touched a machine, and I'd want the company to change that before 2036. It's cheaper than hiring new people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what I'm learning, yes. I wouldn't tell them to leave. Everyone has to decide for themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because buying would vanish before I could get onto the factory floor. What would help is a clear route from office jobs to technical jobs inside the company, with paid training time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to people like my boss, who are fifty and great at something that's disappearing. Young people can retrain, but my boss has spent twenty-five years buying steel and nobody's planning for her.

headlineQuote: Young people can retrain, but my boss has spent twenty-five years buying steel and nobody's planning for her.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old junior buyer** leading a team of five at a car-parts maker's head office.
He's **steady and practical**, uses AI now and then, and has about three months saved.
He is **calm** in the plateau but sees buying named on the Steady Disruption card.
His plan in every AGI picture is a move to the **factory floor**, then a technical skill.
He worries about his **older boss**, who has spent her career in buying.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because buying would vanish before he could reach the factory floor.
